introduction-the-shared-bill-problem.core: A cloud bill is one giant shared check. Without allocation, nobody knows which team, product or customer drove which cost, so nobody feels responsible for optimising it.

first_principles.problem: A $2M monthly bill lands in finance with no breakdown, and every team assumes someone else is the big spender.

analogy.title: A 50-person restaurant bill
analogy.story: Splitting it evenly feels unfair when one table ordered champagne. You need itemised orders per table.
analogy.breaks: Perfect allocation is impossible, so aim for 'good enough to drive behaviour'.

check.q: Why is allocation the foundation of FinOps?
check.a: Without attributing costs to owners, nobody is accountable for optimising them.

the-foundation-tagging.core: Tags are key-value labels on resources (team, service, env, cost-center). Activated as cost allocation tags, they let billing data be grouped by owner and purpose.

first_principles.problem: Thousands of anonymous resources can't be traced to a team or product.
truths: Billing exports include tags once they're activated.
derivation: Define a **mandatory tag set** (owner, service, env, cost-center).

analogy.title: Labels on moving boxes
analogy.story: 'Kitchen – fragile – Alice' tells you where it goes and who owns it, without opening it.
analogy.breaks: Some costs (data transfer, support) can't be tagged directly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every resource from this config is tagged consistently.

check.q: What must you do in AWS for tags to appear in billing reports?
check.a: Activate them as cost allocation tags.

tagging-policies-enforcement-and-inherit.core: Tagging only works if it's enforced. Use org-level tag policies (allowed keys and values), deny untagged resource creation (SCPs, Azure Policy), auto-tag via IaC defaults and inheritance, and remediate stragglers.

first_principles.problem: 'CostCenter', 'cost_center' and 'costcentre' make reports unusable, and 30% of resources have no tags at all.
truths: Some resources inherit context from their parents.
derivation: **Tag policies**: standardise keys, case and allowed values.
**Preventive controls**: deny creation without required tags.
**Inheritance**: account or project-level defaults, propagated tags.

analogy.title: A library that won't shelve uncatalogued books
analogy.story: Books without a proper catalogue label are sent back before they reach the shelves.
analogy.breaks: Hard enforcement can block urgent work, so roll it out gradually with exemptions.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Instances can't be launched without an owner tag.

check.q: What's the difference between preventive and detective tag controls?
check.a: Preventive controls block untagged resource creation; detective controls find and remediate untagged resources afterwards.

the-culture-of-accountability-showback-v.core: Showback shows teams their costs without moving money, which builds awareness. Chargeback actually bills the costs back to team budgets, which builds accountability. Start with showback and mature into chargeback.

first_principles.problem: Teams ignore cost reports that have no consequences, and premature chargeback causes disputes over inaccurate allocation.
derivation: Move to **chargeback** once the data is trusted.
Pair it with **ownership of optimisation levers**.

analogy.title: A household electricity monitor vs. separate meters for flatmates
analogy.story: The monitor raises awareness; separate bills make each person pay for their own usage.
analogy.breaks: Chargeback can create perverse incentives, such as avoiding shared platforms.

example.title: A maturity path

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Teams treat cloud spend like their own money.

example.outcome: cost accountability built into the culture.

check.q: Why start with showback before chargeback?
check.a: Allocation must be accurate and trusted before teams accept being billed for costs.

shared-cost-allocation-the-hard-problem.core: Shared costs (Kubernetes clusters, networking, support, platform tooling) serve many teams at once. Split them fairly by a usage driver (CPU/memory requests, requests served, headcount), or carry them as overhead.

first_principles.problem: A $200k/month shared cluster shows up as 'platform' cost, so product teams appear far cheaper than they really are.
truths: Fair splits need a measurable driver.
derivation: **Proportional**: by usage metrics (K8s requests via Kubecost/OpenCost).
**Even split**: when usage can't be measured.

analogy.title: Splitting a shared taxi
analogy.story: Divide the fare by distance travelled by each passenger, not equally.
analogy.breaks: Idle cluster capacity must be allocated somehow, so decide who pays for slack.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Product teams see their true cost, and over-requesting gets visible.

check.q: What metric commonly drives Kubernetes shared cost allocation?
check.a: Each workload's CPU and memory requests (or actual usage), as measured by tools like Kubecost or OpenCost.

cost-anomaly-detection-the-check-engine-.core: Anomaly detection compares actual spend with expected patterns (ML baselines) and alerts within hours, catching runaway resources, misconfigurations and leaks before the month-end bill.

first_principles.problem: A misconfigured job costs $50,000 over three weeks, discovered only when the invoice arrives.
derivation: Enable **anomaly monitors** (AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, GCP, third-party).

analogy.title: A car's check-engine light
analogy.story: It warns you while driving instead of waiting until the engine seizes.
analogy.breaks: Expected spikes (launches, Black Friday) trigger alerts, so annotate known events.

example.title: A runaway NAT gateway
example.outcome: cost incidents are caught in hours.

check.q: Why is anomaly detection better than month-end review?
check.a: It catches cost spikes within hours, limiting how much money is wasted.

budgets-and-budget-actions.core: Budgets set proactive guardrails: alert at thresholds of actual or forecast spend, and optionally trigger actions (apply restrictive IAM or SCPs, stop instances) when limits are breached.

first_principles.problem: Anomaly detection is reactive, and sandboxes and experiments need hard spending boundaries.
truths: Limits defined in advance prevent surprises.
Some environments can be safely restricted automatically.
derivation: Create **budgets** per account, team or tag.
Attach **budget actions** for sandboxes (deny new resources).

analogy.title: A prepaid card with spending alerts
analogy.story: You get warned as you approach the limit, and the card stops working at it.
analogy.breaks: Automatic actions on production are dangerous, so keep them for non-critical environments.

check.q: Why alert on forecasted spend, not just actual spend?
check.a: It warns you before the overrun happens, while there's still time to act.
